apply_rules generated a silly but seemingly harmless proof term that makes the kernel extremely unhappy to check (it doesn't terminate before I lose patience):

import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Matrix.SemiringInverse

variable (R n : Type*) [CommSemiring R] [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] (A : Matrix n n R)

-- finishes quickly with:
-- set_option debug.skipKernelTC true

theorem ohno
    (h : ∀ {a b : R}, a * A.detp 1 + b * A.detp (-1) = b * A.detp 1 + a * A.detp (-1) → a = b)
    (a b : R) :
    a = b :=
    -- `apply_rules; sorry` generates this
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| sorry

Is there anything that can be done here?
(I would guess that the issue is that the kernel is unfolding detp, but it doesn't look like it has any excuse to do so)

Using 

set_option trace.profiler.useHeartbeats true in
set_option trace.profiler true in

we get

5 h's: [Elab.async] [5301.000000] ✅️ Lean.addDecl ▶
10:    [Elab.async] [50691.000000] ✅️ Lean.addDecl ▶
15:    [Elab.async] [1479921.000000] ✅️ Lean.addDecl ▶
20:    [Elab.async] [47192031.000000] ✅️ Lean.addDecl ▶
25:    [Elab.async] [1509956301.000000] ✅️ Lean.addDecl ▶

Making detp irreducible doesn't help (unsurprisingly I guess, because this is the kernel). I'm about to get on an aeroplane; I'll set the minimiser running on a remote machine and report back when I get home (this looks to me like a good candidate for minimisation although it might be easier to just try a by-hand approach, and also, as it's been noted before, I don't know a way to test that the issue hasn't been minimised away because I don't know how to set an option saying "kernel, fail if you take more than 40M mheartbeats"). BTW the minimiser https://github.com/kim-em/mathlib-minimizer is on v4.28.0-rc1. @Kim Morrison I know you're travelling right now but is there a naive way of bumping this?

It's definitely really slow in the kernel, but it doesn't look to me like it's because it's unfolding detp a lot, since set_option diagnostics true (and set_option diagnostics.threshold 0) shows what it unfolds and it's not much at all

Instead I think it's just an exponentially big proof term to check. Here's the size:
5h: 13279
10h: 433887
15h: 13893343
20h: 444595935
which looks like it gets about twice as big with each h

upd: it can't be just because of the size of the proof term, as Thomas shows
Yeah, to me this isn't terribly surprising because each apply h doubles the size of the goal, no?

Well, maybe not, since the following isn't nearly as bad?

theorem ohno
    (h : ∀ {a b : R}, a + b = b + a → a = b)
    (a b : R) :
    a = b :=
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
    h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
    h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
    h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
    h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| sorry
With 20h, that one has size 75497535, so it's smaller, but not by a lot. (You can check size with set_option pp.exprSizes true)
Yeah, it's still big, but doesn't seem to suffer the same slowness as @Eric Wieser's example?

Changing to 

abbrev left (a b : R) : R := a * A.detp 1 + b * A.detp (-1)
abbrev right (a b : R) : R := b * A.detp 1 + a * A.detp (-1)

theorem ohno
    (h : ∀ {a b : R}, left R n A a b = right R n A a b → a = b)
...

also makes it fast, so that's a temporary solution

It's fragile and cursed: change one character and it goes away.

import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Matrix.SemiringInverse

variable (R n : Type) [CommRing R] [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] (A : Matrix n n R)

--set_option trace.profiler.useHeartbeats true
--set_option trace.profiler true

theorem ohno
    (h : ∀ {a b : R}, a * A.detp 1 + b * A.detp (-1) = b * A.detp 1 + a * A.detp (-1) → a = b)
    (a b : R) :
    a = b :=
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  sorry
  -- [Elab.async] [47192381.000000] ✅️ Lean.addDecl ▶

theorem worksfine
    --                            -> a <- just there in equation below instead of b
    (h : ∀ {a b : R}, a * A.detp 1 + a * A.detp (-1) = b * A.detp 1 + a * A.detp (-1) → a = b)
    (a b : R) :
    a = b :=
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  sorry
  -- [Elab.async] [11486.000000] ✅️ Lean.addDecl ▶
Why is a term with sorry in being sent to the kernel anyway??

Non-mathlib example:

set_option trace.profiler true
set_option trace.profiler.threshold 0
set_option trace.profiler.useHeartbeats true

variable (R : Type) (op : R → R → R) (f g : R)

theorem ohno
    (h : ∀ {a b : R}, op (op a f) (op b g) = op (op b f) (op a g) → a = b)
    (a b : R) :
    a = b :=
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| sorry

(and if you change the b in op b g to an a then the problem goes away). Bhavik points out that perhaps this is things behaving as expected? The term is huge and perhaps there's some trick which simplifies it when you change the b to an a, but in general you have to check the huge term?
perhaps it's the amount of unique subterms

theorem still_slow (h : ∀ {a b : R}, op (op b f) (op a g) = op (op b f) (op a f) → a = b)
    (a b : R) : a = b :=
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  sorry

is still slow with three unique subterms

Kevin Buzzard said:

with three unique subterms

that doesn't sound right, I'm gonna write a code to count how many unique subterms there are
oh they're actually all pretty similar

It seems like the hs are not actually the problem, the problem is the sorry term. When replacing it with sorryAx _ false, typechecking is once again fast (approximately linear in terms of depth) and doing the b -> a replacement doesn't have such a big impact anymore.

And the sorry term is a problem because it introduces a binder! If you didn't know, sorry nowadays elaborates to sorryAx ((tag : Lean.Name) → _) false `source.location.stuff. Not that that entirely solves the mystery though...

Indeed the binder is the trouble:

variable (R : Type) (op : R → R → R) (f g : R)

theorem fast
    (h : ∀ {a b : R}, op (op a f) (op b g) = op (op b f) (op a g) → a = b)
    (a b : R) :
    a = b :=
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
    sorryAx _ false

theorem ohno
    (h : ∀ {a b : R}, op (op a f) (op b g) = op (op b f) (op a g) → a = b)
    (a b : R) :
    a = b :=
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
  h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <| h <|
    sorryAx (Unit → _) false ()

-- note that async elaboration doesn't impact the kernel, and so this still has to wait
example : True := trivial

@Kyle Miller , it seems that this is much more performant if we replace

-sorryAx ((tag : Lean.Name) → _) false `source.location.stuff
+(fun α => sorryAx ((tag : Lean.Name) → α) false) _ `source.location.stuff

(moving the unification out from under the arrow type). Does this looks like a reasonable change, or is there probably an underlying kernel issue here?
